column1: The Beginning of the Trend: Interest Rates  Profits  and Markups

The thesis titled The Beginning of the Trend: Interest Rates  Profits  and Markups by Anton Bobrov and James Traina  published in October 2023  examines the relationship between declining interest rates and the rise in economic profits and markups. The authors argue that the size of these estimates is highly sensitive to the chosen sample start date. Specifically  they find that the increase in markups from 1984 to 2019 is 14% larger than from 1980 to 2019  which translates to a $3000 difference in income per worker in 2019. This sensitivity is attributed to a peak in interest rates in 1984  a period marked by heightened volatility. The authors suggest that researchers should justify their time-series selection and incorporate sensitivity checks in their analyses.

The paper highlights the significant decline in the labor share of value-added and real interest rates since the early 1980s  sparking debates about the implied rise in market power. For instance  Barkai (2020) notes that the decline in interest rates led to a 5 percentage point decline in the cost of capital and a 7 percentage point decline in the capital share  resulting in a 14 percentage point increase in the economic profit share  amounting to over $1 trillion in economic profits in 2014. However  there is substantial disagreement about the growth of economic profits and markups  with different methodologies and samples yielding varying magnitudes.

The authors demonstrate that time-series selection heavily influences the economic size of these results  challenging their robustness. By extending their 4-decade sample back by just four years  they explain 25% of the trend in the real interest rate  37% in the cost of capital  14% in the profit share  and 14% in the aggregate markup. This sensitivity amounts to a $260 billion difference in economic profits in 2019. The authors emphasize that sensitivity is pronounced when analyzing trends using high-volatility time series  such as real interest rates in the 1980s. Data points far from the time value mean or the dependent variable mean have higher influence on time-series regression results. Therefore  points at the beginning or end of a sample are mechanically influential  and points drawn from a highly volatile time series are more likely influential. The volatility in financial markets poses a challenge in accurately quantifying trends  and the authors' empirical contribution indicates this challenge is plausibly significant  calling for justified sample selection and robustness checks.

The authors emphasize the application to quantifying secular trends in market power for two reasons. First  researchers use these different magnitudes to estimate models and inform policies. Following Executive Order 14036  the Council of Economic Advisors (2023) uses evidence from Shapiro (2018) and Philippon (2019) to reorient competition policy. Precise measurements of economic profits and markups are also key targets for modeling and welfare. For instance  Blanchard (2019) cites the scale of rising profits to argue the cost of public debt is small. Second  there is substantial disagreement about the growth of markups. The authors clarify one major reason for these disparate magnitudes: sample selection.

The paper employs the standard methodology of Hall and Jorgenson (1967) to measure the cost of capital using financial-market rates  which track the decline in 10-year Treasury yields. Profits and markups are measured as the residual from national income less payments to labor and capital. The authors calculate the change in the estimated linear trend through 2019 for different start dates in the 1980s. They estimate a simple linear regression for each time series and plot the entire time series at the highest frequency available on the Federal Reserve Economic Data database. They also plot the percentage change in the trend for every starting year in the 1980s compared to a base year of 1980.

The real interest rate is measured as the market yield on U.S. 10-Year Treasury Securities less expected capital inflation  constructed as the three-year moving average of realized capital inflation from the BEA. The linear trend for the real interest rate is steepest when starting the series in 1984  which is the most commonly cited start date in the literature. Data points from the beginning of the sample are highly influential  with the real interest rate being 7 percentage points lower in 1980 than in 1984. The peak in the real interest rate occurred in 1984.

The Hall and Jorgenson (1967) cost of capital formula maps the cost of finance to the cost of capital used in real investment decisions by adjusting it for expected capital inflation  depreciation  taxes  and depreciation allowances. The formula is widely used in the capital investment literature because it holds in a large class of models  relying only on a simple arbitrage argument. The authors use this formula to analyze the impact of declining interest rates on economic profits and markups  highlighting the importance of sample selection in time-series analysis.
